# Understanding the Effects of Mineralization and Structure on the Mechanical Properties of Tendon-Bone Insertion Using Mesoscale Computational Modeling

**Authors:** Zhangke Yang; Daniel Gordon; Yitong Chen; Hui Li; Yongren Wu; Zhaoxu Meng

**Affiliations:** 1.Department of Mechanical Engineering, Clemson University, Clemson, SC 29634 | 2.Department of Bioengineering, Clemson University, Clemson, SC 29634

## Abstract

Tendon-bone fibrocartilaginous insertion, or enthesis, is a specialized interfacial region that connects tendon and bone, effectively transferring forces while minimizing stress concentrations. Previous studies have shown that insertion features gradient mineralization and branching fiber structure, which are believed to play critical roles in its excellent function. However, the specific structure-function relationship, particularly the effects of mineralization and structure at the mesoscale fiber level on the properties and function of insertion, remains poorly understood. In this study, we develop mesoscale computational models of the distinct fiber organization at tendon-bone insertions, capturing the branching network from tendon to interface fibers and the different mineralization scales. We specifically analyze three key descriptors: the mineralization scale of interface fibers, the mean, and relative standard deviation of the local branching angles of interface fibers. Tensile test simulations on insertion models with varying mineralization scales of interface fibers and structures are performed to mimic the primary loading condition applied to the insertion. We measure and analyze five representative mechanical properties: Young’s modulus, strength, toughness, resilience, and failure strain. Our results reveal that mechanical properties are significantly influenced by the three key descriptors, with tradeoffs observed between mutually exclusive properties. For instance, strength and resilience plateau beyond a certain mineralization scale, while failure strain and Young’s modulus exhibit monotonic decreasing and increasing trends, respectively. Consequently, there exists an optimal mineralization scale for toughness due to these tradeoffs. By analyzing the mesoscale deformation and failure mechanisms from simulation trajectories, we identify three fracture regimes closely related to the trends in mechanical properties, supporting the observed tradeoffs. Additionally, we examine in detail the effects of the mean and relative standard deviation of local branching angles on mechanical properties and deformation mechanisms. Overall, our study enhances the fundamental understanding of the composition-structure-function relationships at the tendon-bone insertion, complementing recent experimental studies. The mechanical insights from our work have the potential to guide the future biomimetic design of fibrillar adhesives and interfaces for joining soft and hard materials.

## Introduction

Tendon-bone insertion is a specialized interfacial region that attaches tendon to bone and serves to facilitate joint motion for humans and many mammals. As a transitional region ( < 1 m m ) between tendon and bone (Rossetti et al., 2017), the insertion connects two materials that have rather dissimilar mechanical properties. Specifically, the tendon is relatively compliant or “soft” (Young’s modulus ~ 0.45 GPa in the direction of muscle action) and bone is much more rigid or “hard” (Young’s modulus ~ 20 GPa ) (Genin et al., 2009; Thomopoulos et al., 2012; Wren et al., 2001). Such “hard-soft” material interfaces are known to be subject to increased chances of failure, imputed to increased stress concentrations (Liu et al., 2012). Nevertheless, tendon-bone insertions perfectly address this engineering challenge as they effectively transfer motion and forces between tendon and bone with unexpected durability and the capability of bearing loads that are multiples of the body weight and exert on a broad range of angles.

It has been well appreciated that the biomechanical properties of tendon-bone insertions are largely attributed to their unique structural and compositional features that are intrinsically hierarchical. Specifically, at the sub-millimeter scale, high-resolution figures from microscopic observation reveal that the insertions look more like a discrete structure with splayed fibrillar morphology rather than a continuum material (Deymier-Black et al., 2015; Rossetti et al., 2017; Thomopoulos et al., 2006). The basic unit of the tendon, at the sub-millimeter scale, is the so-called tendon fiber or fascicle. In the insertion, each tendon fiber branches into multiple thinner fibers, which are finally anchored to the bone (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Kannus, 2000; Rossetti et al., 2017). Meanwhile, each tendon fiber is composed of arrays of collagen fibers, which consist of collagen fibrils at the microscale (Benjamin et al., 2006b) (Rossetti et al., 2017). Finally, at the molecular scale, collagen fibrils are assembled by staggered tropocollagen molecules (Baer et al., 1987; Buehler, 2006; Buehler and Yung, 2009). Furthermore, a series of recent studies show that tendon-bone insertions are spatially gradient in composition, structures, and local mechanical properties. Specifically, the collagen fibers stiffen from the tendon side to the bone side, which is attributed to gradient calcification or mineralization (Buehler, 2007; Gautieri et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2014; Wopenka et al., 2008). Moreover, while the collagen fibers at the tendon side are highly aligned, the degree of alignment decreases as the collagen fibers get closer to the bone side (Benjamin et al., 2002a; Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Thomopoulos et al., 2006).

Although tendon-bone insertions are mechanically robust, they can still get injured or even ruptured when being overused or overloaded (Bianchi et al., 2021). Once the insertions are ruptured, it is hard to restore their original function by classical surgical reattachment, i.e., suturing, due to the limited regeneration capacity of functionally and biologically similar structures and compositions to the native anatomy (Atesok et al., 2014; Harryman et al., 1991a; Lui et al., 2010). Deposition of scar tissue also contributes to poor regeneration of the insertion (Lipner et al., 2015; Thomopoulos et al., 2003b). Moreover, the surgically reattached tendon-bone insertions are prone to reinjury in the future (Galatz et al., 2004; Harryman et al., 1991b; Monaco et al., 2010). While restoring the insertion to its natural state remains a significant clinical challenge, it has been indicated that the restoration of its unique structural and compositional features is essential for successful surgical repairs (Chae et al., 2021; Gulotta et al., 2008; Ryu et al., 2020; Tarafder et al., 2019).

A more in-depth understanding of the structure-function relationship of the tendon-bone insertion can advance future surgical and regenerative methods of the tendon-bone interfaces (Kim et al., 2014; Xie et al., 2021). Particularly, the grading mineralization degree and orientation of collagen fibers along the insertion path are critical to the exceptional mechanical properties of insertion (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Genin et al., 2009; Golman et al., 2021; Rossetti et al., 2017; Thomopoulos et al., 2006). To date, some studies have been carried out to understand the structure-function or composition-function relationship of tendon-bone insertion. Thomopoulos et al. (Thomopoulos et al., 2003a) proposed a quasi-linear viscoelastic (QLV) model to quantitatively describe the mechanical properties of supraspinatus tendon-bone insertion. The material coefficients of the QLV model are determined by curve-fitting stress relaxation data with the assumption that collagen fibers are multidirectional at the bony end and unidirectional at the tendon end. Finite element analysis has been carried out to explore how collagen fiber orientation distributions influence load transfer and possibly minimize stress concentration (Thomopoulos et al., 2006). Genin et al. developed a continuum model to predict the elastic properties of tendon-bone insertions given the degree of mineralization and collagen fiber orientation distribution along the insertion (Genin et al., 2009). Numerical simulations have been conducted on an idealized model of the rotator cuff insertion, showing how a compliant tissue interfacial system works to reduce stress concentrations between tendon and bone (Liu et al., 2012). A recent multiscale model based on continuum micromechanics methods was also developed, which utilizes the effective anisotropic stiffness tensor to predict the elastic response of the insertion at different scales (Aghaei et al., 2021).

Despite recent studies, there are critical knowledge gaps in understanding the roles of mesoscale fiber architecture in the overall mechanical properties, deformation, and failure mechanisms of the insertions. A versatile computational model that can capture the unique branched fibrillar structure at the insertions, predict the mechanical properties, and examine underlying mechanisms will be greatly advantageous to fill the knowledge gaps. This work proposes a first-of-its-kind computational model of the tendon-bone insertion in this regard. Specifically, this study employs a mesoscale model to recapitulate the key structural and compositional features of tendon-bone insertions and simulate the mechanical responses under tensile loading from muscle contraction (Roig et al., 2009; Rosenblueth et al., 1958). The mesoscale model builds upon the previously developed elastic network model (Lee et al., 2014; Stein et al., 2011) but has significant improvements in capturing varying fiber diameters and mineralization scales as well as the unique branching structure. We aim to comprehensively investigate the mechanical properties of the tendon-bone insertion under the effects of local mineralization and branching fibrillar structures at the mesoscale. In Section 2, the mesoscale models of the tendon-bone insertion and the simulation methods are described in detail. In Section 3, the simulation results on the effects of mineralization and structure on the mechanical properties of tendon-bone insertion are presented and analyzed. The detailed deformation and failure mechanisms of the insertion model undergoing stretching are examined. Additionally, we present our insights on how natural insertions achieve outstanding mechanical properties and function and discuss future improvements on the model to address certain limitations. In Section 4, the results and conclusions of this study are summarized.

## Model and Methods

### Mesoscale modeling of tendon-bone insertion

We propose a mesoscale computational model building upon our previous works on reduced order modeling of nano/microfibrils (Caviness et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2019) to capture the unique branched fibrillar structure at the insertion, as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). Fig. 1(b) shows an example of the constructed computational model to study the tendon-bone insertion, which has an approximate dimension of ~ 3.6 m m × 0.7 m m × 0.7 m m . Specifically, the mesoscale models include a tendon fiber part and an interface fiber part that splays from the tendon fibers. The tendon part compromises 20 tendon fibers, each of which branches into two interface fibers with an equal diameter, which is ultimately inserted into the bone, as shown in Fig. 1(b). According to previous microscopic characterizations (Rossetti et al., 2017), a tendon fiber may divide into multiple fibers before inserting into bone. In this study, we focus on the two-branch scenario as a representative yet simplified model. However, we note that our model can be straightforwardly modified to consider the multi-branch scenarios, and we believe the results from the two-branch model are translatable to these cases.

We describe both tendon and interface fibers as chains of beads interacting with bonded potentials, as shown in Fig. 1(b), a very efficient and effective method to model fibrils or fibers (Caviness et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021). We discretize both fibers into equal-sized, spherical beads that are tightly connected. As a result, the diameter of the beads is equal to that of the fibers. As a starting point to inform model parameters, we set the diameters of the tendon and interface fibers to be 130.2 μ m and 92.1 μ m ( = 130.2 μ m / 2 ) , respectively, which are consistent with the sizes informed from the experimental observations of the tendon-bone insertion from porcine Achilles (Rossetti et al., 2017). The tendon fibers have a length of 2.6 mm due to computational limitations on model size. However, the length should have a very minor effect on the reported results in this study. The lengths of the interface fibers follow a uniform distribution in the range of 0.5 to 1.5 mm, also resembling the observations from the previous experimental study (Rossetti et al., 2017).

We use the Lennard-Jones (LJ) unit system (Thompson et al., 2022) in the model, which has the advantage of increasing the translatability of the mesoscale model for similar systems, i.e., tendon fibers with different lengths and densities. In this study, we take the unit length in LJ unit to be the diameter of the tendon fiber, i.e., 130.2 μ m or 1.3 × 10 - 4 m . Similarly, the conversion of mass and energy in LJ units to their counterparts in the international system of units (SI) is displayed in Table 1. All the other LJ units are derived quantities from the basic LJ units with the Boltzmann constant k B as 1. For convenience and concision, we use LJ units to describe the computational parameters in the following.

The densities of tendon and bone are about 1.60 g / c m 3 and 1.89 g / c m 3 (Hashemi et al., 2005; Li and Aspden, 1997). There is currently no direct measurement data of the density of the tendon-bone insertion to our best knowledge. Nevertheless, previous studies have shown the insertion is a transitional region where the composition and structure gradually change from tendon to bone (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Genin et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2012; Thomopoulos et al., 2003a). Thus, it is reasonable to assume the density of the insertion to be the average of tendon and bone, i.e., 1.74 g / c m 3 . We note that the density might also vary longitudinally in the insertion region, but a constant density setting is a reasonable simplification considering the minor role played by density. Then, the masses of the tendon and interface beads, which are 8 and 2.828 in LJ unit, are assigned correspondingly to match the density of the system.

In the model, the centers of each pair of adjacent beads in the chains interact through harmonic springs (bonds), as marked in Fig. 1(b). The potential of the harmonic bond is expressed as (1) E b = 1 2 k b r - r 0 2 where k b is the bond coefficient and can be interpreted as the bond stiffness; r 0 is the equilibrium bond length and equal to the bead (fiber) diameters, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). Therefore, we set r 0 to be 1 and 0.707 for the tendon fibers and the interface fibers, respectively.

Cosine/delta angles are employed to account for the bending behavior of the fibers. Specifically, an angle potential is applied to the angle formed by the centers of every three consecutive beads (see Fig. 1(b)), which has the form below. (2) E a = k a [ 1 - cos ⁡ θ - θ 0 ] where k a is the angle coefficient which can be referred to as bending stiffness when θ - θ 0 is small; θ 0 is the angle in radians at which the moment resulting from the angle potential is zero. Generally, θ 0 is set to be π for both the tendon fiber and the interface fiber, as both types of fibers appear to be mostly straight according to experimental observation (Rossetti et al., 2017). We note that this setting may have certain effect on the initial nonlinearity of the stress-strain curves. An exception is that θ 0 is set to π 3 and a very small angle coefficient k a (one-tenth of that of unmineralized interface fiber) is used for angles at the branching points. We have conducted preliminary studies and found that the θ 0 and k a for those angles at the branching points have negligible influence on the simulation results. However, such selections at the branching points help to improve the computational efficiency and robustness. We also note that the torsional behavior of the fiber is not considered in the model since we found the fibers’ torsional property only played a minor role in the insertion structure’s response to tensile deformation.

The modulus of tendon fiber shown in the literature is approximately 0.6 GPa (Deymier et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2014). The modulus of unmineralized interface fiber is chosen to be also 0.6 GPa considering its similarity in composition to tendon fiber. We obtain the bond and angle coefficients by treating the fiber as a cylindrical beam and then using its general force-displacement relation to derive the coefficients. The resulting bond and angle coefficients are shown in Table 2. The details of the derivation can be found in the Supporting Information (SI).

A soft style potential described by Eq. (3) is used for the non-bonded interactions among beads from different fibers. (3) E n = A 1 + cos ⁡ π r r c r < r c where A is a coefficient, r is the distance between two non-bonded beads, and r c is the cutoff distance beyond which the non-bonded force is set to zero. The A and r c are chosen to be 10.0 and 1.0, respectively, which can avoid overlaps between fibers.

### Capturing local mineralization and branching structure in the model

A large body of previous studies has shown that increasing of mineralization scale results in higher stiffness of the collagen fibers (Aghaei et al., 2021; Deymier et al., 2017; Genin et al., 2009; Golman et al., 2021). To quantitatively capture the mineralization scale at the insertion, we introduce a mineralization coefficient ( k ), which serves as the scaling factor for k b and k a of the interface fibers. Therefore, k linearly scales with Young’s modulus of the interface fibers. Basically, a k value of 1 indicates unmineralized interface fibers. Larger k means higher mineralization scale and it leads to a greater Young’s modulus of interface fibers. We only consider homogenized mineralization in interface fibers in this study to focus on the key characteristic that, on average, the interface fibers have a higher mineralization scale compared to tendon fibers (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Schwartz et al., 2012). This approach simplifies our model while enabling an effective examination of this key characteristic.

However, previous experimental studies have observed nonuniform mineralization through the interface (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Schwartz et al., 2012). We also note that there can be mineralization building up in tendon fibers, different from our treatment of unmineralized tendon fibers (Spiesz and Zysset, 2015; Zou et al., 2020). We plan to consider heterogeneous mineralization informed by experimental characterizations in future studies. Our model is designed to be versatile and can be modified to accommodate more realistic scenarios. Specifically, we plan to examine the mineral distributions at tendon-bone insertion in the rat model using a previously demonstrated protocol that simultaneously visualizes collagen fibers and mineralization (Gade et al., 2019).

To study the fracture behaviors of the insertion, we also consider fiber failure using a strain-based criterion. Failure strain ε c r , u is determined to be 0.05 for both tendon fiber and unmineralized interface fiber based on previous experimental results (Deymier et al., 2017). For the mineralized interface fiber, failure strain ε c r , m is assumed to be related to the failure strain of unmineralized interface fiber ε c r , u and mineralization coefficient k through the following Eq. (4): (4) ε c r , m = ε c r , u k

This assumption is in agreement with the experimental observations that insertions with weakened mineralization show lower strength and larger failure strain than those with normal mineralization (Deymier et al., 2017; Golman et al., 2021). Although the choice of ε c r , u and ε c r , m is based on phenomenological assumptions, it effectively captures the primary characteristics of fiber failure. We can incorporate more refined failure strain criteria into our model as additional experimental data become available. Practically, the bonds within the fibers will break if their elongations reach the corresponding failure strain. The numerical solver is set to check for bond breakage every five timesteps as a tradeoff between efficiency and precision.

The initial structures of the insertion model are generated by our in-house code, which specifies two structural descriptors of the interface fibers: average local branching angle ( α - ) and standard deviation of the local branching angle ( σ α ). The local branching angle α is defined as the angle between the orientation of an interface fiber segment and the negative z-axis, as shown in Fig. 1(b). In the following sections, we use the relative standard deviation ( σ α * = σ α / α - ), a dimensionless value, to quantify the scaled degree of dispersion for the local branching angle. Generally, higher σ α * indicates a higher degree of dispersion, scaled by α - . Fig. 1(e) shows a typical distribution of α where α - and σ α * are 13.2 ° and 0.36, respectively. After the initial structures are equilibrated with overlaps being removed, α and σ α * usually experience slight changes from their initial values. Thus, iteration is needed in the structure generation and equilibration processes to reach the desired α - and σ α * . Moreover, since it is quite challenging to control α - and σ α * at precise values, we allow small ranges of both parameters when analyzing their effects on mechanical properties.

### Simulation setup

Given that α - and σ α * can adequately describe the essential architecture of the branching fibers at the tendon-bone insertion, we take them as the fundamental structural descriptors and study their influences on the mechanical properties of tendon-bone insertion. To this end, we build a variety of tendon-bone insertion model structures with different α - or σ α * and then conduct tensile tests on them, mimicking the major loading condition on insertion. Meanwhile, the mineralization scale of the interface fibers is recognized as an essential compositional descriptor. To this end, insertion models with different k are constructed while keeping α - or σ α * as constants as we aim to isolate the effects of mineralization vs. structure.

Then, similar tensile tests are performed to comprehensively evaluate the mechanical properties and failure mechanisms of insertion models with different mineralization scales and structures. The tensile deformation is applied by moving the tendon-end beads at a constant velocity in the z direction while fixing the bone-end beads. The velocity used is 5 × 10 - 4 in the LJ unit, which achieves a good balance between the simulation time and computational stability. We track the total force exerted on the tendon-end beads as the overall force responding to the tensile deformation of the insertion.

All the simulations of this study are conducted in the Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) (Thompson et al., 2022). The timestep is 10 - 3 in all the simulations. Periodic boundary conditions are used in the x and y directions, respectively. Visualization of the simulation results is realized with OVITO (Stukowski, 2010).

### Interpreting tensile testing results.

During the tensile tests, we apply uniaxial stretching to each insertion model until they experience complete failure, i.e., the total force drops to 0. We divide the measured total force by the cross-section area of the insertion model to get the effective tensile stress. A typical stress-strain curve of such tendon-bone insertion models is shown in Fig. 2(a). Five key mechanical properties can be extracted from such a stress-strain curve. Specifically, Young’s modulus ( E ) is obtained by fitting the linear portion of the curve from strain 0 to 0.025, as depicted by the dashed line in Fig. 2(a); the tensile strength ( σ T ) is chosen to be at the highest point of the curve, marked by the circle; the resilience ( u R ) is measured from the area under the elastic portion of the curve as colored in gray; the toughness ( u T ) is calculated from the area under the whole curve, i.e., the region filled with diagonal lines; and the failure strain ( ε f ) is selected to be the strain where the stress drops to zero, as shown by the square.

The extracted five key mechanical properties can be plotted and evaluated using radar charts, as demonstrated in Fig. 2(b), where each mechanical property is represented by an axis of the chart (Niksiar et al., 2021; Porter and Niksiar, 2018). A judicious order of properties (axes) has been shown to minimize subjectivity in multi-dimensional performance comparisons (Albo et al., 2016; Ankerst et al., 1998; Peng et al., 2004). We use the same order as our previous study (Niksiar et al., 2021). We have also examined other orders of axes and confirmed that the trends and results are independent of the order of axes (details in the SI). The innermost and outmost circles in the radar charts represent the minimum and maximum levels of all the five mechanical properties, respectively, among different cases. The areas of the polygons in the radar charts can be used to compare the overall performance in five mechanical properties for each insertion. We will discuss it in more detail in the next section.

## Results and Discussions

In this section, the dependence of mechanical properties of insertion on the key structural and compositional descriptors and the underlying deformation and fracture mechanisms are comprehensively investigated. The major compositional and structural descriptors of tendon-bone insertion are concluded to be k , α - , and σ α * , with k corresponding to the compositional aspect and the other two descriptors related to the structural features.

### Influence of k on the fracture patterns

To study the influence of the mineralization scale of interface fibers on the mechanical properties and failure of the insertion, we gradually increase k from 1 to 5 while keeping α - and σ α * relatively constant, though small deviations are allowed. Specifically, 17 different values of k are used with an increment of 0.25 between 1 and 5. To isolate the effect of k , α - and σ α * are first kept consistent with the experimental observation on the tendon-bone insertion of porcine Achilles (Rossetti et al., 2017). With the image processing software ImageJ (Schneider et al., 2012), we obtained the α - and σ α * as 13 ° and 0.35, respectively. For each k , we generate 5 initial structures for tensile tests to account for the uncertainties during the generation of initial model structures. In actual implementation, we allow small variations in α - and σ α * , which are within the ranges of 12 ° to 14 ° and 0.325 to 0.375, respectively.

A group of snapshots of the insertion models with three k values (1, 1.75, and 5) are shown at two strain levels of 0.04 and 0.1, respectively, during the tensile simulation in Fig. 3. The strain of 0.04 is selected since this is the level of strain when individual fiber breakages and fractures emerge. At strain = 0.1, all the models have reached complete failure. The complete stress-strain curves for these three cases are shown in Fig. 4(a).

Based on the locations where the fracture happens, the failure behaviors of tendon-bone insertion are categorized into three fracture regimes, i.e., interface fracture regime (IFR), hybrid fracture regime (HFR), and tendon fracture regime (TFR). For the IFR, the fracture of fibers only happens in the interface fiber region when the mineralization scale of the interface fibers is low. A representative case exhibiting IFR is the k = 1 case, as shown in Fig. 3(a–b). From the range of k values selected in this study, we find that only the unmineralized interface fiber case ( k = 1 ) shows pure IFR, while slightly increasing k from 1 to 1.25 would lead to HFR. For the HFR, the fracture of fibers happens in both the interface region and the tendon region, which is illustrated in Fig. 3(c–d). From our simulation results, we find that k values ranging between 1.25 and 2.5 give rise to the HFR. For the TFR, fracture of fibers only happens in the tendon region as the interface fibers are overly stiffened by a high level of mineralization, as shown in Fig. 3(e–f). We find that insertion models with k values larger than 2.5 exhibit TFR.

An evident trend observed is that as k increases from 1 to 5, corresponding to increasing mineralization scale in the branching interface fibers, the fracture regime changes from IFR to HFR and then to TFR. In other words, the fiber fracture locations gradually move from the interface fibers to the tendon fibers. Generally, very low mineralization or unmineralized interface fibers result in IFR, medium mineralization scale corresponds to HFR, and high mineralization scale leads to TFR. We note that a high mineralization scale at the branching interface fibers can result from localized calcification, a major pathological change that has been observed at insertions (Benjamin et al., 2002b; Benjamin et al., 2006a; Saran et al., 2024).

It can be observed in Fig. 3 that for TFR, fractures tend to happen predominantly at the rightmost (tendon) end of the model. This is likely due to the inertial effect associated with the high deformation rate and explicit simulation mode used within LAMMPS. Nevertheless, this localized failure mode is believed to have a very minor effect on the trends of mechanical properties to be analyzed next. Moreover, incorporating random defects and property variations along the fibers would be more realistic for studying the failure of insertions and we plan to consider these in our future work.

### Influence of k on mechanical properties

Next, we characterize the five mechanical properties ( E , σ T , u R , u T , and ε f ) for different k values and examine their dependence on failure regimes. The mechanical property data are from five different initial structures to reduce random errors. In the following analysis, we use normalized resilience u R * and normalized toughness u T * by their maximum values measured among all the cases to facilitate comparison.

We note that the stress-strain curves depicted in Fig. 4(a) exhibit only slight nonlinear elastic behavior. The nonlinearity of the stress-strain curve, particularly in the small deformation regime, is influenced by the initial configuration of the fibers. Typically, an initial wavy fiber structure, also common in tendons and insertions, would result in more pronounced nonlinear elastic behavior. Although our model simplifies this by using initially straight fibers, we believe it still effectively captures the key mechanical properties and failure mechanisms of the tendon-bone insertion. This is because the critical mechanical properties and failure mechanisms are most evident beyond the initial nonlinear region of the stress-strain curves.

E shows a monotonically increasing trend with k (Fig. 4(b)). Specifically, it first increases rapidly with k until the middle range of HFR. After that, the uptrend of E slows down, but a nontrivial ascending rate is still visible. The increasing trend of E with k is reasonable since a greater degree of mineralization leads to stiffer interface fibers and, thus, the overall insertion structure. This increasing trend is consistent with the experimental results where increasing stiffness of the tendon-bone insertion is observed with increasing mineralization scale (Deymier et al., 2017; Golman et al., 2021). σ T climbs very fast for k values between 1 to 2 corresponding to IFR and the first half of HFR. A critical point is found in the middle of HFR, after which the σ T saturates with k extending into TFR. The critical point in the middle of HFR corresponds to the case that the strength of the interface fibers reaches that of the tendon fibers, and fracture can happen randomly throughout the fibers. With further increasing of k , the strength of the entire tendon-bone insertion cannot increase beyond that of the tendon part and tends to be saturated when k keeps rising.

The same critical point in the middle of HFR is observed for u R * in Fig. 4(d). A slight difference between the trends of σ T and u R * is that after reaching the critical point, u R * shows a slight decrease in HFR, making the critical point as the maximum. However, a steady plateau of u R * is also observed in TFR. The trend of u R * can be predicted according to the trends of E and σ T . As σ T saturates after the critical point, the continuously increasing E shortens the maximum elastic strain, thus leading to a slightly decreasing trend of elastic energy absorption after the critical point. Fig. 4(e) illustrates the trend of u T * , which displays a clear maximum at the boundary between IFR and HFR. Overall, IFR and HFR, where interface fibers experience fractures, provide higher toughness over TFR, where fracture happens predominantly in tendon fibers.

Lastly, ε f generally shows a decreasing trend alongside k though a large STD is especially evident in the HFR, likely due to the random fractures discussed earlier. We note that for k values corresponding to TFR, the ε f values are significantly lower than those in IFR or HFR, and the overall stress-strain curves exhibit characteristics of brittle failure, as shown in Fig. 4(a) and the k = 5 case. This observation is significant as it indicates that extensive calcification building up in the insertion region could lead to much smaller failure strain and potentially result in premature tearing or damage of the insertion (Deymier et al., 2017; Golman et al., 2021).

We then plot and compare five mechanical properties of tendon-bone insertions with different k values using radar charts (Fig. 5). We note that the mechanical properties used in the radar charts are the average values from Fig. 4. At low k , the shape of the polygon extends horizontally (e.g., the blue polygon in Fig. 5(a)), exhibiting high failure strain and toughness while having low values in other mechanical properties. As k increases, the polygon expands vertically toward high σ T , E , and u R * while shrinking along ε f and u T * horizontally. Ultimately, a narrow triangle shape is formed with large σ T , E , and u R * at high k . A tradeoff exists between the two mutually exclusive groups of mechanical properties, i.e., the group of ε f and u T * and the group of σ T , E , and u R * .

If weights are assigned to each property, an optimal k can be identified that achieves the highest scores under this weighting system. An example is shown in Fig. 5(b), where the normalized areas of the polygons in Fig. 5(a) are plotted against k values. This effectively establishes an area-based evaluation system (Caporaso et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2018). Under this evaluation system, an optimal k is clearly identified around the center of HFR. We also evaluate the performance of the profiles in terms of their first moment of area (Fig. S2(a) in the SI) or with different orders of properties (Fig. S3 in the SI), yielding consistent results. This indicates that HFR is a critical regime for achieving the optimal balance amid tradeoffs. Considering that the center of HFR is where the strength of the interface region matches with that of the tendon region, this likely represents an optimization principle for healthy insertions through the developmental process to achieve the best mechanical robustness. This observation offers valuable insights into designing strong and tough fibrillar adhesives for future engineering applications (Federle, 2006; Li et al., 2016; Murphy et al., 2009).

### Mesoscale deformation and failure mechanisms

In this section, we examine in detail the deformation and failure mechanisms of the insertion at the mesoscale fiber level from simulation trajectories. We select the k = 1.75 case in the HFR since it is around the optimal value in section 3.1. Fig. 6(a) and (b) show the typical bond-based fiber force contours of the tendon-bone insertion model structure before and after fiber fractures happen, respectively. Under tensile loading, the interface fibers exhibit a wider force distribution compared to the tendon fibers, as shown in Fig. 6(c) and (d), which greatly contributes to the dispersed fiber fracture behavior. After some fibers fracture, the forces they previously bore drop to zero, while the forces on the remaining fibers continue to increase until they break (Fig. 6(b), (e), and (f)).

The fractures of the fibers are primarily determined by the force distribution and occur independently of each other. Due to the non-uniform nature of the force distribution, it helps prevent brittle fracture across the entire interface region. Additionally, the observed pattern of fiber fractures helps avoid the formation of an abrupt fracture propagation path, thereby enhancing toughness. In contrast, our previous simulations with non-branched fiber structures showed sudden fractures and much smaller ε f and u T . The observed force distributions and failure mechanisms offer a plausible mechanical explanation for the broadened attachment achieved through branching fiber structures at tendon-bone insertions. The unique branching structure, combined with graded mineralization along the longitudinal direction, is thus considered a key mechanism for the enhanced ductility and toughness of insertions.

### Effect of α - on the mechanical properties

This section aims to study the influence of the mean local branching angle, i.e., α - , which is recognized as one of the two key structural descriptors from a statistical perspective. In this section, we build a variety of tendon-bone insertion structures with α - ranging from 10 ° to 45 ° . While α - varies, σ α * and k are kept relatively constant. Fig. 7(a) shows three typical stress-strain curves of insertion models with low, medium, and high α - , respectively. We select a k value of 1.75 for all the models generated in this section, given that it is the optimal value found in the previous section.

The five mechanical properties, i.e., E , σ T , u R * , u T * , and ε f , are extracted and plotted against α - in Fig. 7(b–f), respectively. Different from the influence of mineralization scale k , monotonic trends are observed for all the five mechanical properties. Specifically, the E , σ T , and u R * decrease with increasing α - , and strong linear correlations are found between α - and E and σ T , respectively. In contrast, u T * and ε f increase with increasing α - .

Fig. 8 shows the kinetics behavior of fiber breakage depending on α - . Specifically, Fig. 8(a) displays the simulation snapshots at strain 0.04 and 0.2 for the tendon-bone insertion model structure with α - equal to 10.9 ° initially. Fig. 8(b) presents the simulation snapshots at strain 0.04 and 0.2 for the tendon-bone insertion model structure with α - equal to 44.6 ° initially. Both snapshots are colored based on the local fiber angles relative to the z-axis during the deformation. Fig. 8(c) and (d) show the corresponding stress-strain curves of the two tendon-bone insertion model structures with α - equal to 10.9 ° and 44.6 ° , in which we also label the bond breaking events for both the interface and the tendon fibers using vertical dashed lines. Based on the fiber breakage locations in Fig. 8(a) and (b) and the bond breaking types in (c) and (d), it can be identified that the entire range of α - , i.e., 10 ° < α - < 45 ° , is under HFR, which means there is no regime transition over the range of α - considered in this section. This accounts for the observed monotonic trends in the five mechanical properties.

Notably, ε f is almost quadrupled when α - increases from around 10 ° to 45 ° . This significant increase in ε f primarily results from the alignment motion of the interface fibers during the tensile deformation. Specifically, in the tendon-bone model structure with a large initial α - (Fig. 8(b)), the angles α of individual interface fibers relative to the z-axis significantly decrease at the strain of 0.2 compared to the angles at the strain of 0.04, as illustrated by the color scales. In contrast, the tendon-bone model structure with a small initial α - (Fig. 8(a)) experiences little to no changes in the angles α when the strain increases from 0.2 to 0.04. Generally, the larger the α - , the more pronounced the alignment motion the interface fibers undergo during tensile deformation, thereby leading to a higher failure strain. The greater interface fiber alignment motions also contribute to more dispersed bond breakages. Fig. 8(c) displays the discrete bond breaking events alongside the stress-strain curve for the insertion structure with an initial α - = 10.9 ° , where the bond breakings are concentrated in a small strain range from approximately 0.04 to 0.05. Conversely, the bond breakings in the insertion structure with an initial α - = 44.6 ° span a much larger strain range (Fig. 8(d)), from 0.05 to nearly 0.2. Therefore, we conclude that more dispersed bond breaking sequences contribute to the enhanced toughness of the insertions.

A similar tradeoff among different mechanical properties is observed when changing α - . Fig. 9(a) shows the radar charts for the five mechanical properties depending on α - . Similar to the observations in Fig. 5(a), the property group of ε f and u T * is competing with the property group of σ T , E , and u R * . Within the considered range, a high α - tends to maximize the ε f - u T * group and minimize the σ T - E - u R * group, while a low α - has the opposite effect. Again, we adopt the area-based evaluation system to screen for the preferred α - value or range. The normalized area and first moment of area of the polygons in Fig. 9(a) are summarized in Fig. 9(b) and Fig. S.2(b) in the SI, respectively. It indicates that the structures with low to medium α - achieve relatively higher scores under the adopted evaluation system.

### Effect of σ α * on mechanical properties

In this section, we investigate how σ α * affects the mechanical behavior of tendon-bone insertions under tensile loading. Given that σ α * is difficult to control at specific values and is correlated with α - , twenty insertion structures have been constructed and categorized into four groups based on their σ α * and α - : 1) low α - and low σ α * , 2) low α - and high σ α * , 3) high α - and low σ α * , and 4) high α - and high σ α * , as shown in Fig. 10(a). Each group includes five independent insertion structures to ensure reliable results. Fig. 10(b) displays the stress-strain curves of the four groups of insertion model structures with relatively low or high α - and σ α * , respectively, where the colored bands represent the ranges of stresses within their standard deviations. It turns out that σ α * has very limited influence on the stress-strain curves when α - is relatively small. Conversely, when α - is relatively large, a high σ α * tends to decease σ T but increase ε f of the tendon-bone insertion structure.

### Discussion on how natural insertions achieve excellent mechanical robustness

Our results indicate that branching structures can fine-tune the mechanical properties of the tendon-bone insertion and work synergistically with local mineralization of interface fibers to enhance mechanical robustness. In natural insertions, there is often a synchronization between local mineralization patterns and branching structures (Aghaei et al., 2021; Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Lu and Thomopoulos, 2013). The tendon typically contains much less mineral content, while the bone is highly mineralized (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Lu and Thomopoulos, 2013), resulting in a lower mineralization scale ( k l o ) on the tendon side and a higher mineralization scale ( k h i ) on the bone side. As a transition zone between tendon and bone, the interface region has an intermediate mineralization scale between k l o and k h i . Based on our analysis, if the interface region had the same σ α * and α - as the tendon region, it would have higher strength due to its higher mineralization scale. This could potentially lead to reduced mechanical robustness. However, studies have shown that both σ α * and α - are actually higher in the interface region compared to the tendon region (Rossetti et al., 2017), which can balance the strength between the interface and tendon regions. This balance enhances ε f and u T * without significantly reducing σ T .

Therefore, the synergistic effect of a graded mineralization scale (Chandrasekaran et al., 2017; Deymier et al., 2017; Lu and Thomopoulos, 2013) and a gradual variation in interface fiber orientation (Lu and Thomopoulos, 2013; Rossetti et al., 2017) observed in natural insertions potentially lead to dynamically matched strength along the entire insertion path, resulting in optimal mechanical robustness across the tendon-bone insertion.

### Limitations of the computational model and future improvements

We acknowledge that the insertion structure modeled in this study is a simplified representation compared to realistic structures observed in natural insertions, which typically exhibit more complex features such as multiple and gradual fiber branching, wavy fiber structure, oblique attachment, and interdigitation along attachment lines. In our future work, we aim to enhance the proposed mesoscale mode to incorporate these features flexibly. For example, gradual mineralization can be modeled by systematically altering the bead types and interactions, with parameters adjusted based on emerging experimental data on the mechanical properties of mineralized collagen fibers. Furthermore, we plan to directly construct fibrillar structures informed by experimental imaging techniques to more accurately capture tendon-bone insertions’ mechanical properties and deformation mechanisms while also seeking direct experimental validation.

Another limitation of the current model is its simplified treatment of fiber failure, which relies on straightforward fiber-breaking criteria and phenomenological assumptions about the failure strains of both tendon and interface fibers. Although this approach effectively captures the primary characteristics of fiber failure, it may overlook the effects of possible plastic deformations in these fibers and the complex dependencies of fiber failure strain on factors such as mineralization and fiber diameter. To address these limitations, we plan to introduce more refined failure strain criteria as new experimental data become available. Additionally, we intend to employ more sophisticated potential forms in our future work to more realistically represent the constitutive mechanical behaviors of tendon and interface fibers.

## Conclusions

This study developed an effective mesoscale computational model of tendon-bone insertion to investigate the effects of mineralization ( k ) and structure ( α - and σ α * ) on its mechanical properties. Through tensile test simulations, we characterized five mechanical properties— E , σ T , u R * , u T * , and ε f —for insertion models with varying mineralization scales and structures. Additionally, we examined the deformation and failure mechanisms at the mesoscale fiber level to yield insights into the intrinsic failure behaviors of tendon-bone insertions.

Our results indicate that as the interface fibers transition from unmineralized to heavily mineralized (with k ranging from 1 to 5), the locations of fiber fracture shift progressively from the interface fibers to the tendon fibers. We categorize insertion failure into three regimes: IFR, HFR, and TFR. The E and σ T of the insertion generally increase with higher k , while ε f exhibits an overall decline with increasing k , albeit with greater variation in HFR. Interestingly, both u R * and u T * initially increase and then decrease slowly, reaching their peak values within HFR. This indicates that specific k values create a dynamic balance between the strengths of the interface and the tendon fibers. By plotting all five mechanical properties on radar charts and evaluating the area, the highest performance occurs around the center of the HFR, underscoring the importance of achieving a balanced strength between branched interface fibers and tendon fibers through moderate mineralization.

The effects of structural descriptors on the mechanical properties of tendon-bone insertions are summarized as follows. When α - is in the range of 10 ° to 45 ° , all insertion failures occur within HFR, displaying monotonic trends for all five mechanical properties. These properties can be categorized into two groups: the first group includes ε f and u T * , which both increase with rising α - ; the second group consists of E , σ T , and u R * , which all decrease as α - increases. These two groups display a clear tradeoff, emphasizing the mutually exclusive nature of the mechanical properties. The influence of σ α * depends on α - . For relatively low α - , σ α * has a minimal effect on the stress-strain curve. However, at higher α - , an increase in σ α * tends to reduce σ T but enhance ε f compared to lower σ α * .

Overall, we believe the findings in this study offer a new level of understanding of the composition-structure-function relationship at tendon-bone insertions. These insights could guide the design of biomimetic fibrillar adhesives or interfaces for joining soft and hard materials. Additionally, the computational models developed for mesoscale collagen fiber structures can be applied to study the structure-function relationships of other soft-hard tissue interfaces that exhibit similar gradual changes in mineralization and fiber structures, such as ligament-to-bone insertions and cartilage endplates (Buchweitz et al., 2024; Lu and Thomopoulos, 2013; Moffat et al., 2008; Quan and Sone, 2015).

## Abstract

Following the explosive growth of global data, there is an ever-increasing demand for high-throughput processing in image transmission systems. However, existing methods mainly rely on electronic circuits, which severely limits the transmission throughput. Here, we propose an end-to-end all-optical variational autoencoder, named photonic encoder-decoder (PED), which maps the physical system of image transmission into an optical generative neural network. By modeling the transmission noises as the variation in optical latent space, the PED establishes a large-scale high-throughput unsupervised optical computing framework that integrates main computations in image transmission, including compression, encryption, and error correction to the optical domain. It reduces the system latency of computation by more than four orders of magnitude compared with the state-of-the-art devices and transmission error ratio by 57% than on-off keying. Our work points to the direction for a wide range of artificial intelligence–based physical system designs and next-generation communications.

## Abstract

An unsupervised photonic generative neural network enables high-throughput image transmission.

## INTRODUCTION

Because of the prevailing development of intelligent society, the transmission of images becomes a fundamental demand in various fields in daily life (1–3). For example, an instant play of one single Blu-ray movie requires a transmission throughput of several gigabits per second. The transmission links require satisfying the throughput of a large number of such terminals simultaneously, which brings extreme challenges for image transmission (4–7). In addition, because image transmission usually requires high throughput and visualization quality, pre- and postprocessing, such as compression and error correction with large operation numbers are essential in image transmission (8–10).

However, although nowadays more than 95% of digital information globally is transmitted through optical fibers (11), image processing remains to base themselves mainly on electronic processors (12, 13). For instance, in an optical fiber communication (OFC) system for image transmission, it includes preprocessing (compression, encryption, and antinoise encoding), electro-optic modulation (EOM), transmission, optical-to-electronic conversion (OEC), and postprocessing (decompression, decryption, and error correction decoding) to reconstruct messages from the received signals (14). Different modulation and demodulation schemes, including pulse amplitude modulation (PAM), phase-shift keying, and on-off keying (OOK), are used to encode and decode the digital signal. The EOM and OEC in an OFC system are usually done by Mach-Zehnder modulators and photodetectors, while the pre- and postprocessing are mostly implemented with digital signal processors (5, 6, 15). Processing the transmitted massive optical image signals, such as encryption and compression, has placed critical burdens on current electronic computing platforms. The gap in the operating frequency between the state-of-the-art electronic circuits and the fiber transmission lines is orders of magnitude due to the limited drift velocity of electrons, therefore becoming one of the most time-consuming parts in high-throughput transmission (4, 7, 16–18).

The recent surge of intelligent photonic computing is considered promising to provide a solution to overcome the electronic bottleneck by processing the images directly in the photonic domain (19–23). Diffractive neural networks (24, 25), coherent nanophotonic circuits (26), convolutional accelerators (27, 28), fiber computing (29–31), and other optoelectronic devices (32–36) successfully realize parallel photonic neural networks and increase the computational efficiency substantially. However, the existing all-optical neural networks are mainly focused on classification tasks, for example, the recognition of handwritten digits and letters. The processing in image transmission requires not only feature extraction and image clustering but also reconstruction after compression and encryption. The recent development of electronic generative models has proved their capability in photorealistic image generation, which is promising for high-quality image transmission (37, 38). In particular, the variational autoencoder (VAE) model can controllably transform between large-scale datasets and low-dimensional representations (the latent space), which finds applications in data encoding and generation (38). Although optoelectronic generative models have been reported, existing photonic intelligent processors are incapable of all-optical end-to-end generative neural networks and, hence, fail in achieving ultralow-latency complicated image processing in transmission (36, 39).

Here, we propose an unsupervised photonic VAE, named photonic encoder-decoder (PED), for end-to-end processing in image transmission. To the best of our knowledge, PED is the first demonstration of all-optical generative neural networks. The end-to-end learned PED structure enables it to encode the optical input information into a compressed and encrypted optical latent space (OLS) for transmission and decode the transmitted distorted signals from the encrypted domain to the reconstructed images optically. The elaborately designed diffractive neurons directly manipulate the information in the optical domain without loss and distortion caused by the convertors to increase the transmission precision. Modeling the transmission noise as the variations in the OLS and constraining it with the probability distribution entitle the PED to learn an optimal coding scheme to maximize its noise resilience. In our prototype optical system, the PED decreases the system latency of image transmission by more than four orders of magnitude compared with the state-of-the-art central processing unit (CPU). On benchmarking datasets, PED experimentally achieves 57% reduction in transmission error ratio (ER) than OOK, one of the mainstream methods with the lowest ER. In addition, the PED increases the transmission throughput by two orders of magnitude than PAM-8 and 87 times than the conventional compression method discrete cosine transform (DCT), as we demonstrate in medical images.

## RESULTS

### Modeling of the PED

In the proposed PED architecture (Fig. 1A), the input messages are encoded into an OLS with an optical artificial neural network encoder and are later correspondingly coupled into the single-mode fiber bundle. The noise during transmission is modeled as the variation in the OLS in a VAE-based architecture. An optical artificial neural network decoder decodes the transmitted latent space representations, i.e., the combination of the Gaussian speckles after the collimating lenses, for the faithful reconstruction of input messages. Because the OLS highly encrypts the input messages, it prevents tapping and guarantees the security of transmission.

Figure 1B is the system design of the all-optical PED, establishing the encoding-transmission-decoding flow without the requirement of any analog-digital/digital-analog and opt-electrical conversions by carrying out all processes in the analog optical field, which notably improves the speed and efficiency of communication. As depicted in Fig. 1B, after an all-optical encoder composed of trainable diffractive layers, the PED passively couples the light field into a fiber bundle through a lens array and decodes the OLS with an all-optical decoder back to the original data. Every lens in the lens array couples one corresponding area of the optical field to one single-mode fiber in the fiber bundle. The coupling efficiency depends on the light field and the characteristics of the fibers and lens. The light field in the fiber can be considered as a linear superposition of different spatial frequencies with respective coupling coefficients (see Materials and Methods for the modeling of the coupling process). In addition, PED is naturally compatible with most existing OFC systems as they both use single-mode fiber bundles for transmission, which are already buried underground over the world (see details about the compatibility in note S5).

The PED allows two operation modes: general and data-specific modes, as shown in Fig. 1 (C and D, respectively). The general mode provides fundamental secure and noise-resistant transmission for arbitrary images optically. When some prior information is obtained, not necessarily labels, the data-specific mode additionally allows notable compression to improve the transmission throughput.

The latent space of the VAE architecture is a hyperspace representation of inputs that is subject to a continuous distribution function (38). In the PED, we generate and evaluate the OLS by dividing the output plane of the encoder into subregions and sum the low-frequency component of the optical field at each subregion by coupling it into a single-mode optical fiber. Different subregions correspond to different single-mode fibers of the fiber bundle. The number of subregions, which corresponds to the number of optical fibers for spatial multiplexing, determines the dimensionality of the OLS. After transmission, the OLS is collimated into the optical decoder to reconstruct the inputs.

Arbitrary images are encoded into binary bits and transmitted on the basis of OOK in the general mode, while applying a pretrained non–data-specific PED provides photonic encryption for image transmission as the encoder embeds the information into the OLS. High precision can be achieved simultaneously with the noise-resistant coding scheme optimized by the PED. To facilitate the evaluation of PED performance, we capture the output intensity of each layer to reuse the spatial light modulator (SLM), named optoelectronic PED. Optoelectronic and all-optical PED have comparable performance, as proved in fig. S5 (see Materials and Methods for the details of experimental modeling and setup). The letters (“VER”), digits (“191”), and Chinese characters are effectively encrypted beyond recognition. The OLS produces the coupling relationship between all latent values, which makes interception with only some of the channels relatively impossible.

## DISCUSSION

By effectively extracting features from the original images, PED achieves orders of magnitude higher throughput compared with existing methods in image transmission. On the medical dataset, PED improves the transmission throughput by 232.3 times, 77.4 times, and 87.1 times compared with PAM-8, QAM-512, and DCT when achieving the same transmission fidelity experimentally (see note S3 for calculation details). In the general mode, because the PED solves the bottleneck of system latency by all-optical processing, its bit rate theoretically achieves 24.6 Tbit/s (see note S4 for calculation details). In addition, adjusting the parameters in the network helps further improve the performance of PED. We analyze the four main parameters that influence the performance of the PED, which are the layer number of the encoder/decoder (fig. S7A), the diffractive distance between the layers (fig. S7B), the diffractive distance after the last layer in the encoder/decoder (fig. S7C), and the pixel size, i.e., size of neurons (fig. S7D). The performance of the PED improves notably when the layer number of the PED decoder increases from 1 to 2 and grows gradually when the layer number continues to increase for both general and data-specific modes. For the distance between the diffractive masks, 15 cm achieves the best performance for both general and data-specific modes. The performance of the PED increases as the diffractive distance after the last layer of the encoder/decoder increases in the range of 10 to 50 cm. The PED shows better performance with smaller pixel sizes in the range of 10 to 25 μm.

Simultaneously, the all-optical PED experimentally improves the computation latency by five orders of magnitude than the state-of-the-art CPU (Intel, CA, Intel Core i7 6500U CPU @2.5 GHz). In addition, we calculate the end-to-end system latency of PED in a fiber communication system, including computation, opt-electronic conversions, and analog-to-digital converters (fig. S11), and the PED improves the system latency by more than four orders of magnitude than the state-of-the-art CPU. It shows that the PED optimizes the time-consuming bottleneck that restricts the improvement of throughput instead of some parts that are fast enough already. Even when compared with the state-of-the-art graphics processing unit (GPU) with ultra-high computing speed (~47 TOPS/S) (43), PED remains to achieve one order of magnitude improvement in system latency (see note S3 for calculation and measurement details). We note that the commercial image communication systems can only achieve a computing speed much lower than this example with the state-of-the-art CPU or GPU considering the cost. Therefore, the actual improvement may be higher.

Compared with existing optical neural networks, the PED extends the application beyond decision-making tasks to notably wider generative scopes. Figure S4 demonstrates applications of the PED as a universal unsupervised optical generative model in style transferring and human action video enhancement. Because decision tasks and labeled images are only a small portion in real life, the demonstration of an unsupervised generative photonic model with ultra-high speed and the ability of parallel computation will be capable of revolving plenty of application fields, including augmented reality, edge computing, and virtual reality.

In conclusion, we propose an unsupervised PED for OFC. It not only provides an end-to-end learned processor for image processing in OFC, including encoding, encryption, compression, and decoding all optically but also improves the communication quality by processing in the optical domain directly. Two modes of the PED have introduced: the general mode for arbitrary image coding and encryption and the data-specific mode for notably high throughput. The transmission ER experimentally decreases by 57% by the PED, as demonstrated on a benchmarking dataset. The PED widens the transmission throughput by two orders of magnitude than PAM-8 and 87 times than DCT over displayed medical images. The all-optical PED reduces the system latency by more than four orders of magnitude compared with the state-of-the-art CPU.

By codesigning the encoder, decoder, and fiber system all in the optical domain, our work makes inherent connections between the unsupervised learning architecture and the physical model of fiber communication systems, inspiring the next-generation all-optical communication systems with higher throughput, accuracy, and data security. We believe that the proposed generative photonic computing system and the end-to-end unsupervised photonic learning method will facilitate a wide range of artificial intelligence applications, including 6G, medical diagnosis, robotics, and edge computing.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### PED modeling and training details

We use a VAE architecture to establish the PED, which is one of the most mainstream unsupervised generative models with various application scopes (38). The encoder-decoder structure perfectly matches the OFC process, and its ability to reconstruct data from a low-dimensional domain enables the PED to compress and encrypt the transmitted information. In addition, the VAE provides better performance in noise resistance due to the variation in latent space when training. The loss function of the PED for optimization can be described as L = α l KLD + β l MSE + γ l OP where lKLD is the Kullback-Leibler divergence that guarantees the distribution in the OLS close enough to the ideal distribution, i.e., Gaussian distribution; lMSE is the mean square error between the PED output and the input; and lOP is a penalty term. To prevent the middle results from changing fiercely between the diffractive layers to make the images sick or sensitive to noise, we use an optical penalty term in the loss, similar to what many electronic deep neural networks do (44). lOP is usually composed of an l1- or l2-norm between the middle results and the ideal output; α, β, and γ are constant coefficients that balance these losses.

We use the optical fields in the fibers to characterize the high-dimensional latent values in the optical networks. The all-optical PED encodes the information in both the amplitude and phase domains. During training, the phase and amplitude are calculated on the basis of the optical field in front of the coupling lens array with corresponding complex coupling coefficients. For experimental convenience, we also establish the model of optoelectronic PED. It allows the PED to achieve comparable performance with only one phase modulator. The output of each diffractive layer is captured with a sensor, and the measured intensity is fed back to reuse the diffractive system. In this way, the optoelectronic PED achieves nonlinearity from the sensor but loses phase information to encode. Figure S5 presents the comparison of the performance between the all-optical and optoelectronic PED on both general and data-specific modes. The all-optical and optoelectronic PED achieves tantamount results in the reconstruction fidelity and noise resistance. In addition, the latency of this reusing architecture in optoelectronic PED has been proved ultra-low (45). Therefore, the optoelectronic PED provides a convenient way to validate the all-optical PED. More details for the experimental implementation in Figs. 3 and 4 are included in the “Experimental setup” section below.

During training, the proposed OLS complies with the assumption of a biased Gaussian distribution because the intensity of the optical signals is nonnegative. The deviation is set as a constant instead of learning during training to mimic the real fiber communication situations. Adjusting the deviation to different values helps the PED handle different noise levels. The phase masks for the general and data-specific modes are shown in fig. S6.

### Experimental setup

The system design and experimental setup are shown in fig. S2. We use a single-mode 532-nm laser (Changchun New Industries Optoelectronics Tech. Co., Ltd., MGL-III-532-200 mW) to generate the collimating incident light. A cascaded beam expander system is used to expand the diameter of the beam to ~25 mm. We use an amplitude-modulation SLM (HOLOEYE Photonics AG, HES6001) to generate the grayscale input and a phase-only SLM (Meadowlark Optics Inc., P1920-400-800-PCIE) as the diffractive layer in the optical neural network. It has a frame rate of up to 714 Hz. The pixel size of the optical neurons that we use in the PED is 18.4 μm. A 4f system is placed between the two SLMs to conjugate the input image onto the phase modulation plane. The diffractive distance between the second SLM and the sensor is 300 mm. We use a scientific complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (Tucsen Photonics Co. Ltd., Dhyana 400BSI) to measure the intensity output from the optical neural network. In the optoelectronic PED, the multilayer network is realized by iteration with this system. The coupling of the fiber is measured in sequence by one fiber to mimic the effect of the array (fig. S2C). An equivalent experiment of all-optical PED is demonstrated in fig. S15, which shows similar exceeding performance to optoelectronic PED. The long-distance transmission noise is simulated according to the SNR as modeled in the Supplementary Materials. We use the single-mode fiber (Daheng Optics, DH-FSM450-FC) at 532 nm.

### Adaptive training of the PED

The layers in the PED should be aligned precisely, or the signal cannot be processed with the correct corresponding weights. In an integrated all-optical PED shown in Fig. 1B, it is aligned with the high-resolution microscope and fixed with bonding, which has submicrometer alignment precision. For evaluation setup with commercial devices, the alignment precision depends on the precision of the translation stages (Daheng Optics, GCM-930602 M), which provides an alignment error below 6 μm in PED. The PED has the robustness to small misalignment errors and, for larger alignment errors, we use adaptive training to correct some of the errors in the experimental system. By retraining the last few diffractive layers with experimental middle outputs over a small scale of the training dataset, adaptive training achieves distinct improvement on the test dataset. Because of the leverage of reconfigurable equipment in the setup, we can easily change the weight in the PED after adaptive training.

#### General mode

Because the training and testing datasets are the same and the scale is small, we go through the whole dataset (512 instances). The noise is randomly added in each training epoch. Adaptive training fine-tunes the decoder masks for several epochs over data with random noise.

#### Data-specific mode

We experimentally test the output of the encoder on a small part of the training dataset (~3%) and fine-tune the decoder with this small amount of training data.

### Modeling of the coupling in the PED

The corresponding lenses in the microlens array divide the light-field output from the encoder into m areas, where m is the dimensionality of the OLS. Each lens Fourier transfers the corresponding area to its frequency domain on its Fourier plane. Given single-mode fibers with a proper numerical aperture, only the low frequencies are coupled into the fibers. The light in the fiber is a combination of light with different incident angles with corresponding complex coupling coefficients. The coupling efficiency is based on the data because the nonplanar wavefront affects the coupling. Figure S8 (A and B) gives an example of the modulated light field on the front focal plane and the results after coupling by the lens array. Light with different incident angles has different complex coupling coefficients.

In this work, we simulate the complex coupling coefficients at different incident angles with the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method (fig. S8C). In this way, any complicated incident wavefront can be decomposed into components from different angles to add up.

We take the vertical incidence as an example to verify the FDTD simulation with theoretical predictions. We use the Gaussian approximation of the zeroth-order Bessel function. The electric field of the fundamental mode on the edge is (46) E ff = 2 π ω 0 exp [ − ( r ω 0 ) 2 ] where r is the radial coordinate and ω0 is the radius of the single-mode field. The coupling efficiency is usually defined as (46) η = ∣ ∬ E if ∗ E ff d s ∣ 2 ∬ ∣ E if ∣ 2 d s ⋅ ∬ ∣ E ff ∣ 2 d s , where Eif is the electric field of the incident light on the back focal plane and Eff is the electric field on the fiber edge. The FDTD simulation corresponds well with the theoretical result in this example.
